claim: Amazon Ads' setup advice: run automatic and manual campaigns together, one product group and one category per campaign, no end date, about $10 a day to start, and move winning search terms from the auto report into manual.
body: Amazon Ads' Sponsored Products best practices describe a simple structure. Create manual campaigns to supplement an automatic one rather than choosing between them. Set no end date (always on), and in the first week check metrics at least twice. Ad groups can hold up to 1,000 products, and Amazon suggests advertising at least two products. The loop that makes the structure work is the search term report: download it from the automatic campaign, find the shopper queries that produced sales, and target those terms in a manual campaign with match types you control, adding negative targeting where terms waste spend. How to apply: launch each new ASIN with one automatic campaign and one manual campaign of its known keywords, review weekly, and harvest converting terms into manual exact while negating them in auto so the two do not bid against each other.

claim: Sponsored Products automatic campaigns split into four targeting groups (close match, loose match, substitutes and complements) that can be bid separately, so the vague auto campaign can be steered.
body: Amazon Ads' targeting guide explains that an automatic campaign is not one black box but four groups. Close match shows the ad to shoppers using search terms closely related to the product. Loose match shows it for loosely related terms. Substitutes shows it on detail pages of similar products, competing for the same purchase. Complements shows it on detail pages of products that go with yours. Each group can be switched on or off and bid on its own. This matters most for a new ASIN: close match usually converts best and deserves the highest bid, loose match finds new query ideas at a lower bid, substitutes tests whether shoppers will switch from a named rival, and complements can work for accessories (a proofing basket next to a bread knife) but is often weak for primary products. claim: In manual Sponsored Products campaigns, bid highest on exact match, lower on phrase and lowest on broad, as Amazon Ads recommends, because exact queries are the most relevant and broad buys reach.
body: Amazon Ads' targeting guide defines the three keyword match types. Broad match gives the widest exposure, matching related shopping queries. Phrase match is more restrictive and generally gives more relevant placements, with the keyword's words in order inside a longer query. Exact match matches the search term word for word, same words in the same order. Amazon's own advice for manual bids is to set the highest bid on exact, a lower one on phrase and the lowest on broad. The logic is cost per order: an exact query like silicone bread proofing basket converts better than a broad cousin, so it can carry a higher click price for the same return. Keywords are limited to 10 words and 80 characters and cannot contain question marks, slashes, double quotes, ampersands or backslashes. Amazon also says to test match types for at least one to two weeks before pausing keywords. How to apply: put each core keyword into all three match types in separate ad groups, bid them in descending order, and after two weeks keep the match type that delivers orders at or below your target ACOS.

claim: Amazon defines ACOS as ad spend divided by ad revenue times 100 and ROAS as its inverse; $50 spent for $100 in ad sales is 50% ACOS and a ROAS of 2.
body: Amazon Ads' ACOS guide sets the two efficiency measures for sponsored ads. ACOS (advertising cost of sales) is ad spend divided by ad-attributed revenue, times 100. ROAS (return on ad spend) is ad revenue divided by ad spend, the inverse. The worked example: spending $50 to earn $100 gives an ACOS of 50% and a ROAS of 2. Amazon says there is no single good ACOS, that ACOS should not be the only metric watched, and that new campaigns often show a high ACOS simply because they are new. Both figures count only sales Amazon attributes to the ads, so they ignore organic sales the ads may lift and the profit left after product cost and fees. How to apply: report ACOS by campaign and ASIN against a target set from margin (see the break-even card), read new-launch ACOS over weeks rather than days, and add a whole-business view such as total ad spend over total sales before cutting campaigns that look expensive alone.

claim: TACoS divides ad spend by total sales, organic included: $100 of ads with $100 of ad sales is 100% ACoS, but with $900 organic sales on top it is a 10% TACoS.
body: TACoS (total advertising cost of sales) is a seller-community metric, not one Amazon defines in its ad documentation. Helium 10's explainer gives the formula as advertising spend divided by total revenue, times 100, and contrasts it with ACoS: $100 of spend producing $100 of ad-attributed sales is 100% ACoS, yet if the same product also sold $900 organically, total sales are $1,000 and TACoS is 10%. The point is that ACoS judges a campaign, while TACoS judges how dependent the whole product or store is on advertising. A falling or flat TACoS while sales grow suggests ads are lifting organic rank and sales; a rising TACoS with flat total sales means the business is buying the same revenue at a higher price. The article gives no good TACoS number, so the target has to come from the product's margin. How to apply: track TACoS monthly per ASIN beside ACoS; during launch accept a high ACoS if TACoS trends down as organic sales arrive, and treat a TACoS that keeps rising for several months as the signal to fix the listing or price, not just bids.
conditions: Amazon products with both ad-attributed and organic sales; monthly view.
fails_when: Organic sales are driven by outside traffic (social, email) rather than ad-lifted rank, so TACoS falls for reasons unrelated to Amazon ads; seasonal swings distort a single month.

claim: Amazon counts an FBA item as excess once it has over 90 days of supply against forecast demand, and its guideline is to hold 30 to 60 days of expected sales.
body: Amazon's inventory performance page lists what drives the Inventory Performance Index (IPI). Four categories: avoid excess and aged inventory, improve 90-day rolling sell-through, fix stranded listings, and keep popular items in stock. An item is excess when it has more than 90 days of supply based on forecasted demand; the excess inventory percentage is the share of FBA units so marked. Sell-through rate is units shipped over the past 90 days divided by the average units on hand in that period. Stranded inventory is sellable stock in a fulfilment centre with no active listing, which costs storage with no chance of sales. FBA in-stock rate is the share of time replenishable ASINs were in stock over the last 30 days, weighted by units sold in the last 60 days, and the Restock today button flags SKUs whose days of supply are below restock lead time. Amazon's guideline is to keep enough stock to cover 30 to 60 days of expected sales. How to apply: set reorder points so FBA stock stays between roughly 30 and 60 days of sales, keep the rest upstream (own warehouse or AWD), and clear stranded units weekly.

body: Amazon's Product Opportunity Explorer, available to Professional sellers in Seller Central under Growth, is built to judge unmet demand for new product ideas. claim: When comparing ideas in Google Trends, compare topics rather than single terms where possible; terms miss misspellings, synonyms and plural forms, while a topic groups one concept across terms and languages.
body: Google's Trends help on comparing terms sets the rules. The current Explore lets a user compare up to 8 groups of terms at once, with up to 50 terms in each group (classic Explore allows 5 groups of 25). A search term matches the words typed in the chosen language: one word also returns phrases containing it, several words return results containing each word in any order, and quotation marks restrict results to the exact phrase. The plus sign combines terms into one line, such as two languages for the same word. Terms do not pick up misspellings, spelling variations, synonyms, or plural and singular versions, so a single term can understate interest. Topics are groups of terms sharing one concept in any language, for example London including Londres. Non-Latin terms may return little data where most people search in English. How to apply: compare product ideas as topics when Trends offers one; when it does not, build a group with the plural, singular and common synonyms joined by plus signs, keep the same region and time range for every idea, and read the shape of the line (rising, flat, seasonal), not its absolute value.

claim: A Google Trends line at or near 0 means too little search volume to show, and low-interest lines are mostly noise; do not read a spike in a tiny niche term as rising demand.
body: Google's Trends FAQ explains why small terms behave badly. Trends only shows data for popular terms, so terms with low search volume appear as 0. Because the data is a sample of searches, some noise is always present, and Google says it is most noticeable on queries with low or no search interest, where lines jump around for random reasons. Trends also removes repeated searches from the same person over a short time and filters out queries with apostrophes and other special characters. Graphs for 30 days or longer use UTC with daily, weekly or monthly points, while seven days or less use local time and hourly points. For product research this means a niche idea whose Trends line is mostly zeros with occasional spikes has no readable trend at all, and a single spike is likely noise, not a breakout. How to apply: before trusting a Trends signal, widen to the broader topic or category term and a multi-year window; if the specific term is still mostly 0, size demand with a volume tool (Keyword Planner, Amazon's Product Opportunity Explorer) instead, and only call a trend when the line rises across several periods.
conditions: Google Trends for niche or long-tail product terms.
numbers: graphs of 30 days or longer use UTC; 7 days or shorter use local time

claim: In the US, a smoke test that takes orders for a product you may never make must follow the FTC's dry-testing conditions: say it is only planned and may not ship, notify buyers if dropped, refund promptly and never substitute.
body: The FTC's guide to the Mail, Internet or Telephone Order Merchandise Rule covers testing demand for merchandise that does not exist yet, which it calls dry-testing. A seller may do it only if five conditions are met: the promotion makes no suggestion that the item will be shipped or that interested customers will receive it; every promotional material discloses all material aspects, including that the merchandise is only planned and may not be shipped; if any part of the promotion is later dropped, buyers are told within a reasonable time; if no decision to ship has been made within a reasonable time, buyers are told and offered the chance to cancel, with a prompt refund where they paid; and no other merchandise is substituted for what was ordered. If the conditions are not met, the full rule applies, with its shipping deadlines. A fake buy button that takes money with no disclosure is not a smoke test under this guidance; it is an order. How to apply: run demand tests as a clearly labelled waitlist or reservation (planned product, may not ship, refundable), collect emails or deposits only on those terms, and set a decision date after which you either ship or refund everyone.

claim: US pre-orders must ship within the time you state, or 30 days if you state none; when late, get the buyer's consent to a new date or refund within seven working days of cancellation.
body: The FTC's Mail, Internet or Telephone Order Merchandise Rule applies to pre-orders once money is taken. A seller must ship within the time clearly stated or, with no statement, within 30 days of receiving a properly completed order (payment plus the information needed), and must have a reasonable basis for any shipping promise, based on expected demand, supply, fulfilment capacity and records. When the seller learns it cannot ship on time, it must seek the buyer's consent to the delay before the promised date; a first delay notice with a new date of 30 days or less can treat silence as consent. If consent is not obtained, the seller must refund all money for unshipped goods without being asked. Refunds are due within seven working days after cancellation, or within one billing cycle for credit sales where the seller is the creditor. Factory delays are common on a first production run, so a pre-order campaign with a tight ship date turns a supplier slip into a legal deadline. How to apply: state a ship window that includes production, freight and inspection plus buffer, write the delay-notice email before launch, and keep a cash reserve to refund every pre-order if the run fails.

claim: Amazon says ACOS must stay below the profit margin to make money, so an idea's margin before ads is its break-even ACOS; at ACOS times price you know the ad cost each ad-driven order can bear.
body: Amazon Ads' ACOS guide states that to maintain a profit, ACOS needs to be lower than the profit margin, and that the first step is working out break-even ACOS before setting a target. ACOS is ad spend divided by ad sales. That turns into a screen at the idea stage. Take the target price; subtract landed product cost, marketplace or payment fees, fulfilment and an allowance for returns; the share left is the margin before advertising, which is also the break-even ACOS. Whatever share that is, each ad-attributed order can carry ad spend up to that share of the price before the sale loses money. If research suggests launch campaigns in the niche will run near or above that level, the product only works if organic and repeat sales carry it. Amazon adds that new campaigns often show high ACOS simply because they are new. How to apply: for every shortlisted idea, compute margin before ads at the target price, write it down as break-even ACOS, and drop or re-price ideas whose break-even sits below the ACOS you expect during launch.

The highest include backpacks, handbags and luggage at 12.8%, compact appliances 12.6%, eyewear 12.1%, watches 12.0%, full-size appliances 11.9%, computers 11.4%, consumer electronics 11.2%, jewellery 10.8% and pet products 10.2%. The lowest include grocery and gourmet at 2.9%, office products 4.4%, toys and games 4.7%, and beauty, health and personal care 5.5%; home and kitchen sits at 8.1% and sports and outdoors at 8.7%. claim: Big parcels carry carrier surcharges on Amazon's US return labels: UPS adds handling over 50 pounds or 48 inches, and a large package surcharge with a 90-pound minimum billable weight past 96 inches long or 130 inches length plus girth.
body: Amazon's page on seller-fulfilled return shipping costs passes on carrier rules that make bulky products expensive to take back. UPS bills the greater of actual or dimensional weight (length times width times height divided by 139 inches) plus a fuel charge that typically runs 13% to 15%. An additional handling surcharge can apply when a package weighs more than 50 pounds or its longest side exceeds 48 inches. A large package surcharge applies when the longest side exceeds 96 inches or length plus girth (twice the width plus twice the height) exceeds 130 inches, and such packages have a minimum billable weight of 90 pounds. Adjustments can post two to three weeks later. For product research this is a second cost of size beyond outbound fulfilment: each return of a big, light product is billed on box volume, not weight. How to apply: for any idea in a large box, compute its dimensional weight at the 139 divisor, check it against the surcharge limits, and cost an expected return label into the margin; a product that crosses 48 inches or 50 pounds needs either a high price or a near-zero return reason.
conditions: Seller-fulfilled returns in the Amazon US store; carrier rules also shape own-site returns.

claim: A seasonal product stocked at Amazon for winter pays peak storage: $2.40 per cubic foot a month for standard items in October to December against $0.78 in January to September.
body: Amazon's storage fee page shows how much the calendar matters for seasonal products. Before the February 2027 change, standard-size items pay a base of $0.78 per cubic foot per month in the off-peak period (January to September) and $2.40 in the peak period (October to December); oversize items pay $0.56 and $1.40. Sellers past their first year with high storage utilization pay a surcharge on top, up to a total of $4.28 per cubic foot in peak for standard items. A product whose demand peaks in winter is therefore stored at the much higher peak rate exactly when it is needed, and anything left after the season sits into the next year as aged stock, which the new age-based fee charges more for after six months. For product research, a strongly seasonal idea needs a margin that covers peak storage and an exit plan for leftovers. How to apply: read the idea's Trends line over several years to time the peak, plan to land stock just before it, size the order to sell through within the season, and plan a markdown or removal for the remainder before it ages.
conditions: Amazon US FBA storage before 1 February 2027; age-based rates after that.

claim: Budget about $50 to $100 per supplier sample plus express air freight for a product retailing at $20 to $50, ask for the sample cost to be credited against the bulk order, and expect several sample rounds.
body: Alibaba.com's buyer guide on samples says a sample is usually one unit used to check quality, materials and colour before a large order, and also a test of how the supplier communicates. Some suppliers let buyers tick a box on the product page; otherwise the buyer writes the request, introducing the company, giving almost the same product detail as a full order, and including the shipping address. The buyer normally pays for the sample and shipping; some suppliers waive the cost if they expect a large order. The guide's estimate is about $50 to $100 for a sample plus express air shipping when the product retails for $20 to $50, varying with distance, and buyers can ask for the sample cost to be deducted from a later full order. Factory samples ship quickly; custom samples take longer because they are built to the buyer's spec, and samples often differ from mass production, so several iterations may be needed. Payment should go through Alibaba.com rather than outside platforms. How to apply: order samples from several shortlisted suppliers at once, budget for more than one round on the chosen one, and approve a production sample before paying the deposit on bulk.

claim: On Alibaba.com, negotiate MOQ, samples, price and customisation through Contact Supplier or Chat Now, prefer Verified or Trade Assurance suppliers, and make counter-offers near the asking price rather than a fraction of it.
body: Alibaba.com's official buyer guide lays out the path from search to order. Ready to Ship listings can be bought directly with Start Order, but samples, orders below the minimum order quantity (MOQ), lower prices and customisation all need negotiation through Contact Supplier and the Chat Now messenger. It names three supplier identifiers: Gold Supplier; Verified Supplier, whose profile, management system and production capability have been assessed or inspected by third parties; and Trade Assurance suppliers, who accept payment through Alibaba.com's payment portal. The guide advises keeping the transaction on Alibaba.com, mentions its Product Inspection Services, and recommends ordering samples, especially for private label or customised products, before buying in bulk. On negotiation it gives an example: for a $10 unit, offering $7 or $8 on a 1,000-unit order is reasonable, while offering $2 is not. Suppliers often sell samples at the retail price. How to apply: shortlist Verified or Trade Assurance suppliers, open with a sample request and a realistic first-order quantity, ask what MOQ the quoted price assumes, and counter within a credible range.

claim: Set the pre-shipment inspection at AQL 2.5 for general consumer goods with zero critical defects: for 4,000 units at General Inspection Level II, sample 200 and accept the lot only if 10 or fewer fail.
body: QIMA, an inspection company, explains Acceptable Quality Limit sampling, based on ISO 2859 and ANSI/ASQ Z1.4. AQL sets the most defective units a random sample may contain before the whole lot is rejected, and is set separately for each defect type. QIMA says AQL for critical defects (safety or legal failures) is commonly 0; AQL 2.5 is the most common standard for general consumer goods; AQL 1.0 is used for higher-risk categories; and AQL 4.0 where minor cosmetic defects are acceptable. Its worked example: a shipment of 4,000 units inspected at General Inspection Level II gives code letter L; code letter L at AQL 2.5 calls for a sample of 200 units; if 10 or fewer fail the batch passes, and 11 or more means rejection. The value of agreeing these numbers is that pass and fail are defined before production, so a failed inspection is a contract matter, not an argument. How to apply: write the AQL levels (0 critical, 2.5 major, 4.0 minor, or stricter for children's or electrical products) and the defect list into the purchase order, and book the inspection before the final payment.
conditions: Bulk production runs from contract factories; random sampling of finished goods.

claim: In the US, any product designed mainly for children 12 or younger needs a Children's Product Certificate based on tests by a CPSC-accepted third-party lab, and importers must e-file certificates from 8 July 2026.
body: The US Consumer Product Safety Commission's page says domestic manufacturers and importers of children's products must issue a written Children's Product Certificate based on test results from a third-party, CPSC-accepted laboratory. A children's product is a consumer product designed or intended primarily for children 12 years of age or younger, and those subject to a children's product safety rule need third-party testing and certification. The certificate has seven elements: the product covered, each applicable safety rule, the manufacturer or importer, contact details for whoever keeps the test records, date and place of manufacture, date and place of testing, and the lab (or a small-batch registration number). From 8 July 2026, importers of most regulated consumer products must file certificates electronically with US Customs and Border Protection. This adds lab fees, time and paperwork to every children's product idea, and the costs repeat with material or supplier changes. How to apply: when an idea could be seen as for children (toys, kids' cups, baby items, small decorative items), decide early whether it is a children's product, get lab quotes into the landed cost, and drop ideas whose margin cannot carry testing.

claim: At the idea stage, look up the US duty rate in the Harmonized Tariff Schedule or the USITC database, treat it as approximate since CBP makes the final call, and get a binding ruling when the margin depends on it.
body: US Customs and Border Protection's guidance on duty rates says the Harmonized Tariff Schedule gives duty rates for virtually every item, but classifying an item correctly takes expertise: details such as fibre content, construction and country of origin change the rate. The USITC Tariff Database gives an approximate rate, only as accurate as the information entered. CBP makes the final determination of the correct duty rate, not the importer, and for very specific duty information on a particular item an importer can request a binding ruling; local ports can also advise. For a product idea, duty is one of the few landed-cost lines that can move the margin by many points, and additional duties on top of the base rate can apply by origin, so a guess made from a similar product can be wrong. How to apply: for each shortlisted idea, find the likely HTS code and base duty, check for additional duties for the planned origin country, add duty to the landed cost on the cautious side, and for any product where a different code would break the margin, request a binding ruling before the first order.

body: Jungle Scout's 2024 seller report surveyed nearly 2,000 Amazon sellers and businesses between 1 December 2023 and 3 January 2024, focusing on 1,064 sellers with at least one live listing. Among small and mid-size sellers, 57% reported profit margins higher than 10%, 28% above 20%, and 13% said the business was not yet profitable. On timing, 22% were profitable within three months, 16% in three to six months, 20% in six months to a year, 11% in one to two years and 2% after more than two years, so 58% were profitable within the first year. These are self-reported net figures from a tool vendor's audience, which skews toward active, committed sellers. They are useful as a reality check on a plan: a model that assumes a margin well above 20% from month one sits above what most sellers report. How to apply: when building the plan for a new product, treat roughly 10% to 20% net margin as the normal range, show the month the product turns profitable, and test the plan at a margin below 10% to see whether the cash still lasts.

A demand estimate taken from the top three listings in a niche is the ceiling, not the expected result. claim: In Jungle Scout's January 2025 survey of nearly 1,500 Amazon sellers, 38% named higher shipping costs as a top challenge, 34% rising cost of goods and 32% growing ad costs: stress-test every idea's margin on all three.
body: Jungle Scout's State of the Amazon Seller 2025 surveyed nearly 1,500 Amazon sellers and businesses from 10 to 27 January 2025. The top challenges were cost pressures: 38% cited higher shipping costs, 34% said they struggled with the rising cost of goods, and 32% said growing advertising expenses were a concern. The report also says fewer businesses source from China while sourcing from the US has nearly doubled, without giving exact shares. For product research this argues for testing margins against cost increases rather than today's quotes: freight, unit cost and click prices are the three lines most sellers saw rise, and a product with a thin margin at current costs is the first to break. How to apply: for each shortlisted idea, rerun the unit economics with freight, landed unit cost and cost per click each raised by a set stress amount, and drop ideas whose margin turns negative under the combined case; favour ideas whose price can absorb increases without leaving the niche's price band.

claim: In the US, a general-use product covered by a CPSC safety rule needs a General Certificate of Conformity from its maker or importer, based on testing or a reasonable testing program; third-party lab testing is not required.
body: The US Consumer Product Safety Commission's page on the General Certificate of Conformity says domestic manufacturers and importers of certain general-use products, meaning products not made primarily for children, must issue a written certificate under section 14(a) of the Consumer Product Safety Act when the product is subject to a CPSC rule or similar requirement. The certificate must be based on testing or a reasonable testing program; unlike children's products, third-party laboratory testing is not required, though a certifier that relies on a third-party lab must name it. The certificate has seven elements: the product, each CPSC rule it is certified to, the certifying manufacturer or importer, contact details for whoever keeps the test records, date and place of manufacture, date and place of testing, and any third-party lab used. From 8 July 2026 importers of most regulated consumer products must file certificates electronically with US Customs and Border Protection. For a private label importer, the importer is the certifier, not the factory. How to apply: for each idea, check whether any CPSC rule covers the product type; if one does, plan who tests, budget for it in the landed cost, and have the certificate ready before the first shipment is entered.
